author: reek
body: `int-rem` is the truncating remainder: it takes the sign of the DIVIDEND, and it is what `idiv` leaves in RDX with no correction applied. It is the remainder that pairs with `/`, which truncates toward zero, so for every pair the identity

author: reek
body: holds -- including when either operand is negative. That identity is the reason this builtin exists; before it, the only remainder Codex exposed made the identity false for every negative dividend.

author: reek
body: `int-mod` is Euclidean: its answer is never negative, whatever the signs of the operands. It does not pair with `/` and is not meant to. It is measured in the same rows here so that the two contracts are legible side by side and so a change to one that disturbed the other would be visible.

author: reek
body: Both operands arrive as parameters at every call site. A literal dividend folds at compile time, which would measure the constant folder rather than the emitter; a literal divisor takes the power-of-two strength reduction, which is a different path again. `rem-computed` exists to reach the standard emit path -- the reg-locals fast path fires only when both operands are plain locals -- so both paths of the builtin are covered rather than only the quick one.
